title: SEA GATE
canon: Present-day Brooklyn, high summer: Sea Gate, the real private gated town at the western tip of Coney Island — water on three sides, its own armed police, one manned boom gate where the biggest city in America stops. Fraud investigator Jim Lang comes through the gate after his whistleblower client is drowned in a foot of basement water, and stays to turn the men who stole the storm-recovery millions against each other — a contemporary RED HARVEST (Hammett, 1929, public domain) where Mary Dwight walks out clean and Lang's death is the price. NRC feature; formerly titled TSUNAMI, now canonically SEA GATE.
look: Daylight noir in July: hard vertical sun, glare off sand and clapboard, heat shimmer, a flag dead still. The look is the hundred-foot contrast — Coney Island's carnival roar (Wonder Wheel, boardwalk neon, packed beach) against the silent, storm-scarred, moneyed streets behind the fence. Nights are lit only by what is really there: ride neon, sodium lamps, guard-booth fluorescence, police light bars. Hard, dry, anti-romantic — nothing golden, nothing nostalgic.

stills.notes: EXT. PETE'S STAND - DUSK (opening sequence). 'They grab each other across the counter, the half-hug of men who hugged for real exactly once, at a funeral, and decided that was the lifetime allotment.' / PETE: 'Look at you. You got old.' / JIM LANG: 'I got old. You got wide.' Why: the whole friendship — twenty years in a Plymouth, forty years of saved stools — lands in one awkward grab across a clam counter. Jim ref only; Pete is not established cast.
stills.prompt: The counter of a tiny hand-painted clam stand on the Coney Island boardwalk, Brooklyn, July, dusk. Two old men grab each other across the counter in a stiff half-hug: a heavyset man in his mid-forties, rumpled grey summer suit, tie loosened, and the stand's owner, a big happy man in an apron over a faded baseball shirt, wiping rag still in one fist. Their faces pass over each other's shoulders, eyes shut a half-second too long for men who only joke. Forty years of yellowed snapshots taped to the wall behind the counter. Light: dirty pink dusk sky over the packed beach, the stand's one bare bulb already burning warm against the blue, the Wonder Wheel's first lamps coming on behind them, mixed temperatures everywhere. Full-bleed frame, no black bars.

stills.notes: INT. CONDEMNED HOUSE, BASEMENT - NIGHT. 'He crouches a long moment, eye level with the dead man.' / JIM LANG: 'You had clams on Tuesdays. Pete liked you. That counts for more than you'd think.' / 'On a nail in the joist above the water, just out of a drowning man's reach: a child's orange life vest, dry as a bone.' Why: not the crime scene — the eulogy. A man talking quietly to a body nobody else will mourn is the moment in time; distinct from the old body-alone shot.
stills.prompt: The basement of a condemned, storm-wrecked house inside Sea Gate, Brooklyn, night. A heavyset man in his mid-forties in a rumpled grey summer suit crouches on the lowest dry step, forearms on his knees, eye level with a drowned man lying face-down in two feet of black standing water — his lips parted mid-sentence, talking quietly to the body as if it can hear him. On a nail in the joist above the waterline hangs a child's orange life vest, bone dry. Light: only his flashlight, set down on the step beside him, one hard low beam skating across the black water and up the peeling plaster, the vest catching the edge of the beam, everything outside it falling to nothing. Full-bleed frame, no black bars.

stills.notes: INT. CLOSING OFFICE - NIGHT (first meeting). JIM LANG: 'I'll take the paving material.' / 'She hands him the cup. Their hands almost touch. They both clock it.' Why: the love story starts here, in a cup of terrible coffee — two guarded people both noticing the half inch between their hands and neither saying it.
stills.prompt: The counter of a small storefront title office inside Sea Gate, Brooklyn, night. A woman around forty — sharp-eyed, reading glasses pushed up into her hair, sleeves rolled — passes a cup of burnt coffee across the counter to a heavyset man in his mid-forties in a rumpled grey summer suit. Their fingers stop a half inch apart on the cup, and both of them are looking at the hands, not at each other. Survey maps on the wall, lien folders stacked to the ceiling, a little radio, a percolator gone black on its burner. Light: tired ceiling fluorescents greening the room, one warmer desk lamp pooling on the maps, a faint stain of boardwalk neon through the front glass — three temperatures that do not match. Full-bleed frame, no black bars.

stills.notes: EXT. BEACH EDGE - GOLDEN HOUR. 'Jim stops walking. So does she. The light is all over both of them.' / JIM LANG: 'Right now I forgot to.' / 'The lemonade drips. She doesn't look away.' Why: the exact instant the con stops being a con — a look held too long, admitted out loud, nothing touching but the light.
stills.prompt: The rail at the beach edge of the Coney Island boardwalk, Brooklyn, the last hour of a July day. A woman around forty in a cardigan over a summer dress and a heavyset man in his mid-forties in a rumpled grey summer suit have stopped walking and stand facing each other a foot apart, a paper cup of frozen lemonade melting down her hand, neither one looking away — the look held too long to be anything but the truth. Light: the sun low and flat off the water, hard on one side of each face and gone on the other, the ocean going purple behind them, two gulls lifting off the rail, the boardwalk crowd dissolving into glare down the planks. Full-bleed frame, no black bars.

stills.notes: EXT. FLOODED STREET - DUSK. 'She steps in front of him, sets the grocery bag on the wet asphalt, takes his face in both hands. A can rolls out of the bag and stops against the curb in the black water.' / MARY: 'Look at me. Not down the street. You put them there. Didn't you.' / 'She hits him in the chest, once, with the flat of her hand, no force, the way you knock on a door you know is locked.' Why: the accusation and the love in the same grip — her hands on his face while he tries to look past her at the armed porches he made.
stills.prompt: A storm-scarred residential street inside Sea Gate, Brooklyn, dusk. A woman around forty stands in the middle of the wet asphalt holding a heavyset man's face in both hands, pulling his eyes down to hers — he is mid-forties, rumpled grey summer suit, and he is still trying to look past her down the block. Her grocery bag sits on the road beside them, one can rolled out against the curb in a black skim of old floodwater. Far behind them, soft, a man sits on a porch with a shotgun across his knees. Light: the sky gone ash-blue, porches falling to shadow, the only warmth the far gold blaze of the Coney Island rides and food signs past the fence a hundred feet off. Full-bleed frame, no black bars.

stills.notes: INT. MOTEL ROOM - NIGHT. MARY: 'G-I-M. She's three.' / 'Jim Lang sits with the rust on his hand and the tray with his name spelled wrong. He does not eat it.' / 'The door swings. The box fan moves the foil but not the heat.' Why: the whole choice in one object — a three-year-old's foil tray of peppers on one side, rust from the south gate boom on his hand on the other, and he does not reach for the tray.
stills.prompt: A cheap motel room off Neptune Avenue, Coney Island, Brooklyn, night. A heavyset man in his mid-forties sits alone on the edge of the bed in a rumpled grey summer suit, the door just closed on him, staring at a foil-covered dinner tray on the dresser with a name written across the foil in a child's fat marker letters: G-I-M. A smear of rust crosses the heel of his open upturned hand. A box fan in the window lifts one corner of the foil and drops it. Light: the parking-lot lamp cutting hard and cold through the half-open curtain, a thin pink wash of far ride neon along one wall, the bedside lamp off, most of the man fallen into shadow. Full-bleed frame, no black bars.

stills.notes: INT. CONDEMNED HOUSE, BASEMENT - NIGHT (the rescue). 'He pulls her in. Holds her. The bulb hums.' / MARY: 'You son of a. You bought me a soda.' / 'On the stairs, above the waterline, a child's orange life vest. Bone dry. On its nail.' Why: the one embrace in the film, held in the same water the story started in — her ruined evidence floating around their feet, the dry vest above them, nothing needing to be said.
stills.prompt: The basement of a condemned house inside Sea Gate, Brooklyn, night. A heavyset man in his mid-forties in a rumpled grey summer suit stands shin-deep in black floodwater holding a woman around forty hard against his chest — her shoes gone, blood dried at her hairline, her fists closed in the back of his jacket, her eyes shut. At the foot of the stairs a banker's box lies on its side, its title files gone soft and grey in the water. Above them on the stairs, on a nail, a child's orange life vest, bone dry. Light: one bare bulb on a wire, humming, throwing a single greasy stripe of reflection across the still water, the bowed plaster walls falling off into dark on every side. Full-bleed frame, no black bars.

stills.notes: EXT. SEA GATE - SOUTH GATE - PRE-DAWN. 'Mary stands in the headlamp light on the boardwalk. Clean. Dry. A citizen. She turns back to the fence.' / 'Mary's hand goes to the chain link, fingers through the steel.' / MARY: 'I'd have drunk it with you. The stupid orange.' Why: the goodbye she never got to say, said to a dark she cannot see into — one hand in the steel is the entire ending. Distinct from the old walk-out shot; this is the moment before she can walk.
stills.prompt: The public side of the dead south gate of Sea Gate, Brooklyn, pre-dawn. A woman around forty stands close against the chain-link fence with the fingers of one hand pushed through the steel, an overnight bag on her shoulder, a small cut at her hairline, her lips moving — saying something quietly into the dark on the other side, where nothing shows but the black shapes of silent houses. Behind her, two idling NYPD cruisers throw their headlamps across her back and print the diamond shadow of the fence over her and up the wire. Light: only the cruiser headlamps and the first grey of dawn coming up over the flat Atlantic, the Wonder Wheel a dark unmoving ring far down the boardwalk. Full-bleed frame, no black bars.
